hero.headline: Build SEO Super Pages with structure, not one giant prompt
hero.answer: A strong AI SEO Super Page starts with a reusable page schema, then generates each section, image, FAQ, and quality check independently. This keeps the output inspectable, easier to improve, and less likely to sound like a generic AI article assembled from repeated filler phrases.
summaryBullets: Plan the page as structured blocks before writing paragraphs.
Use provider-neutral model routing so content can move across Codex, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Kimi.
Treat image prompts and image QA as first-class article assets.
Block publishing until SEO, factuality, tone, and image checks are visible.
hero.trustCue: Research prototype updated on 2026-04-28 with explicit quality gates and mock generation evidence.

sections.heading: Start with a Super Page schema before writing
sections.searchIntent: The reader wants to understand what separates a Super Page from an ordinary long-form blog post.
sections.summaryClaim: A schema makes the page inspectable and prevents the writer from producing an unstructured wall of SEO text.
paragraphs: The first useful step is not asking a model to write a complete article. It is defining the page contract: what the hero answer must prove, which sections satisfy search sub-intents, where images are needed, which internal links support topical authority, and what quality gates must pass before publishing.

This approach gives the team a reusable structure that can be validated before any expensive model call runs. If a generated outline lacks FAQs, image slots, metadata, or internal links, the system can fail early with a precise error instead of letting a weak article reach the editor.
examples: For a software comparison page, the schema can require a decision table, best-for labels, caveats, and a final recommendation checklist.
caveats: The schema should guide quality without forcing every keyword into the same rigid layout.
qualityNotes: Every section maps to an explicit search sub-intent and quality note.

sections.heading: Rewrite each block with context and constraints
sections.searchIntent: The reader wants a practical way to make AI content feel less generic.
sections.summaryClaim: Independent block rewriting makes it easier to add examples, caveats, and source notes without repeating the same AI cadence.
paragraphs: A block-based rewrite pipeline gives each section its own intent, source notes, examples, and anti-AI-tone constraints. The model does not need to invent a full article arc every time; it only needs to improve a focused block while preserving the page plan.

The reviewer can then reject mechanical openings, unsupported statistics, fake citations, or paragraphs that repeat the same rhythm. This is harder to enforce when the entire article is produced as a single response, because failures are mixed together with otherwise usable sections.
examples: A section about image quality can require one concrete artifact checklist: distorted hands, unreadable text, plastic textures, impossible reflections, and generic stock-photo framing.
caveats: Block rewriting still needs source discipline; smaller prompts do not automatically make factual claims reliable.
qualityNotes: Section includes concrete examples and avoids vague SEO filler.

sections.heading: Make image generation part of the article plan
sections.searchIntent: The reader wants to know how image prompts can improve SEO content quality and user trust.
sections.summaryClaim: Article images should explain the topic or demonstrate a workflow, not merely decorate the page.
paragraphs: Image generation works better when the article schema stores the image purpose, prompt context, realism constraints, avoid-list, alt text, caption, provider, and QA status. The image is no longer a disposable illustration; it becomes a reviewed article asset with provenance.

For AI SEO pages, the most important prompt details are usually mundane: plausible environment, real tools, natural lighting, readable composition, and explicit avoidance of fake interface text. These constraints reduce the visual AI smell that makes generated blogs feel cheap.
examples: Instead of asking for 'SEO dashboard image', ask for a realistic editorial photo of an analyst reviewing content briefs, with no readable UI text and no floating holographic icons.
caveats: Some topics are better served by diagrams or annotated screenshots than photorealistic hero images.
qualityNotes: Image prompt contains explicit realism constraints and avoid-list.

sections.heading: Show quality gates before publishing
sections.searchIntent: The reader wants assurance that AI output will not be published blindly.
sections.summaryClaim: Visible quality gates make the tool more trustworthy for both developers and editors.
paragraphs: A useful open-source SEO writing tool should show what passed, what failed, and what still needs a human decision. The publish state should not hide weak factual support, missing alt text, duplicate canonical URLs, or images marked for regeneration.

The quality report should live with the article artifact so teams can reproduce why a page was considered ready. This also makes model experiments easier because each provider can be compared against the same acceptance criteria.
examples: A quality report can mark tone as pass, image relevance as warn, and citation coverage as fail, blocking a publish-ready label until the failure is resolved.
caveats: Quality gates are guardrails, not a replacement for editorial judgment on high-risk topics.
qualityNotes: Quality states are visible and cannot be collapsed into a false publish-ready state.

faq.question: Why not generate the full SEO article in one prompt?
faq.answer: One-shot generation is fast, but it makes structure, factuality, image planning, and tone review harder to inspect. Block generation allows targeted retries and clearer quality gates.

faq.question: Can this pipeline use models other than Gemini?
faq.answer: Yes. The intended model gateway is provider-neutral, so content tasks can route to Codex/OpenAI-compatible models, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, or mock adapters.

faq.question: How do images reduce the AI feel of a blog page?
faq.answer: Useful images show specific workflows, objects, or diagrams that support the article. Storing prompts, captions, alt text, and QA status helps avoid generic stock-photo visuals.
